Many parameters other than temperature and dissolved oxygen show variations over depth as a result of the strong thermal stratification that develops in Jocassee reservoir (Figures 2-18 and 2-19). These include nutrients, pH, alkalinity, hardness, specific conductance and iron. The effect is particularly great in the deeper portion of the hypolimnion where dissolved oxygen levels approach zero and reducing conditions produce large changes in some parameters.
Lake Jocassee fish flesh has been found to contain high levels of mercury (Sherer, 1975; Abernathy, 1975). Sherer (1975) and Abernathy (1975) have reported mercury levels in largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) that are above the maximum methylmercury limit for edible portions of fish of 0.5 ug/g set by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). High mercury levels have also been reported in other Lake Jocassee fishes. Mercury levels in fish in excess of the FDA maximum level have also been reported for Lakes Keowee and Hartwell, located downstream of Lake Jocassee (Abernathy, 1975, citing Carter, 1973, and Knowles, 1973).
Abernathy (1975) and Sherer (1975) report a mean concentration of 3.01 ug/g in fish sampled from August 1973 through May 1974. Other fishes collected in early 1975 contained mercury levels ranging from less that 0.01 to 1.86 ug/g. Mercury data supplied by the South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control for the period March 1975 to early 1976 show mean values of mercury in fish from Lake Jocassee and Lake Keowee (Table 2-7). These later data show lower mercury levels in largemouth bass than the earlier data, with a mean value of 1.12 ug/g. Mercury levels appear to be decreasing with time in Lake Jocassee fish, although further study will be necessary to confirm such an assessment.
Abernathy (1975) concludes that "consumption of bass from Lake Jocassee is inadvisable." All fish samples analyzed by Dr. Abernathy exceeded the FDA maximum level for fish.
